newsitem.title: UK: Impala chairman "quite bullish" for platinum.
newsitem.headline: Impala chairman "quite bullish" for platinum.

text.p: There were grounds for being "quite bullish" about platinum prices in the medium term, Michael McMahon, chairman of Impala Platinum Holdings saId on Friday.
This was despite Russian sales from stock "topping up the market and being responsible for the sogginess of the market," he said at a company presentation.
"The past four or five years of weakness of the market is a factor of them topping up shortfalls," McMahon said.
However the "consensus" in the industry was that the Russian stocks were of "quite finite duration".
"In the medium term I am quite bullish", he said.
Over the coming few months however, the platinum price would be influenced more by speculation than factors of supply and demand.

"There is no sense of real movement in the next few months. May be it (the price) is too low just now but that is because of disenchantment by North American speculators and is not Russian driven," he said.
Platinum fixed at $384.25 per ounce on Friday just above the lowest fixing since January 28, 1994 of $381.50 touched three days earlier.
McMahon said before the company considered re-opening the monthballed Messina and Barplats properties, it would need to be certain that a higher market price was sustaInable.
"We are at least 25 percent away from what would be necessary," he said.
The current price was squeezing margins which were at their lowest for eight-10 years, he said.
Impala currently had a 15 percent operating margin which was just above break even given the need for capital expenditure.
But by reducing operating costs by five percent annually, the margin could be increased to 33 percent by the year 2001.

Impala's received income from the "basket of platinum group metals it mined and sold had fallen from over $700 per ounce two years ago to about $500 this year and was "indicative of the pressure we are under", McMahon said.

Productivity had been increased through reducing the work force from 52,000 to 31,000 over the past four years leading to the output per man month climbing to near the levels at the Lonrho and some of the Rustenburg mines.
McMahon explained that the proposed merger of platinum interests between Impala and Lonrho was critical to reducing the working costs at the Impala mines.
It was vital to maximise the relationship with Lonrho. "The staus quo is not attractive to any of the players," he said.
An appeal against the European Union (EU) decision in April to block the merger could be heard in three-four months.

The reason the merger was blocked by the EU was the area in the merger holding structure where Impala's parent company Gencor Ltd and Lonrho would have joint control of the expanded Impala through equal 32 percent shares, he said.
McMahon said "defensive" currency hedges which Impala had entered last year to protect its bottom line had led to opportunity losses after the rand fell against the U.S. dollar.
By the end of this month, Impala would be "completely out" of its defensive currency hedges.
After that the normal policy of hedging only the immediate receivables would be continued, he said.
